name: Laennec monaural stethoscope and mediate auscultation
summary: Laennec used a listening cylinder at Hôpital Necker in 1817, published a wooden design in 1819, and by January 1820 the editor of a London medical journal had obtained cylinders from Paris and arranged for copies.
description: Laennec’s method of listening to sounds of the chest through a cylinder for diagnosis. He described trying rolled paper before adopting a bored wooden instrument and developed the method through repeated bedside observations and comparison with autopsy findings at Hôpital Necker.
tier_reason: Prefer2 for the original Forbes local-use witness; current main has already broadened the identity and added1819 evidence, so do not apply this old-scope rank blindly. This is a scoped consequence judgement, not a reward for documentation or representation.

impact.note: Listening to the chest became a new diagnostic ability for physicians across many societies, with improved stethoscopes as successors; implies tier 1, above the narrower-scope reviewed tier 2.

date.label: 20 December 1817
date.basis: Laennec dates the admission to 19 December 1817 and says the cylinder examination took place the following day.

events.statement: At Hôpital Necker in Paris, Laennec listened to a patient’s lungs and heart through a cylinder and used what he heard in forming a diagnosis.
events.scope: One bedside examination in Laennec’s service at Hôpital Necker.
events.caveats: The case report calls the instrument a cylinder without specifying its construction. The examination date refers to this case.

evidence.supports: Laennec records that a patient admitted to Hôpital Necker on 19 December 1817 underwent cylinder examination the following day.

evidence.locator: Printed pp. 221–222, case-note sample from Fonds du Musée Laennec, folder I, lot b
evidence.supports: A separate December 1817 case in notes kept by the Necker interns also documents mediate auscultation.

date.basis: Paris imprint on the title page of volume I of the original edition.

events.statement: In Paris, Laennec published his method of mediate auscultation with a description and drawings of his wooden stethoscope.
events.caveats: The treatise made the method available to readers. Its publication date measures access to the text.

evidence.locator: Volume I title page, §§11–13 (pp. 9–11), and plate I
evidence.supports: The 1819 Paris edition describes the bored wooden cylinder, its joint, and its end fitting, and illustrates the instrument.

evidence.locator: L’édition originale and the collection description
evidence.supports: Institutional library identifies the first edition and date and records a model stethoscope of 1819.

date.label: By January 1820
date.basis: The January 1820 review reports that the editor had already obtained the cylinders from Paris.

events.statement: By January 1820, the editor of London’s Medico-Chirurgical Journal had obtained stethoscopes from Paris and arranged for Mr. Alnutt in Piccadilly to make copies.
events.place_note: The journal identifies Paris as the source of the instruments and Piccadilly as the site of local manufacture.
events.scope: Physical transfer of Laennec-type cylinders to a journal editor and an arrangement to reproduce them locally.
events.caveats: The journal gives an offer price and an upper bound for transfer. The specific supplier, transfer date, sales and scale of use remain unknown.

evidence.supports: The editor reports obtaining cylinders from Paris and arranging for Mr. Alnutt in Piccadilly to make them at four shillings each.

contributions.resource: Obtained Paris cylinders and arranged local reproduction.

date.label: 28 May 1822
date.basis: Forbes dates the case to 24 May and the stethoscope examination to the 28th.

events.statement: Forbes examined a patient with a stethoscope in his Chichester Dispensary practice on 28 May 1822.
events.scope: Monaural stethoscope used for mediate auscultation in John Forbes’s Chichester practice.
events.caveats: This is one practitioner’s use, not the first British use or general adoption.

evidence.supports: Forbes reports a stethoscope examination on 28 May 1822 during the same Chichester practice.

earliest_record.rationale: Laennec’s 1819 treatise dates a clinical cylinder examination to 20 December 1817. The introduction reports an earlier, improvised trial with a paper roll in 1816. The form used in the December 1817 case is unspecified and the printed description attests the wooden design in 1819.

community_entry.community: Laennec’s clinical service at Hôpital Necker in Paris
community_entry.rationale: Laennec’s dated case shows use of the cylinder in a bedside examination. Independent reading of the service’s manuscript notes documents the method in another case that December.
community_entry.caveats: The dated case supports use in Laennec’s service. Uptake outside that service is evidenced separately.

caveats: Three distinct stages have dates here. The 1817 case describes clinical use of a cylinder. The 1819 book publishes a specific wooden design. The January 1820 London review reports physical transfer and a local supplier.

research.note: The first French edition is the primary source for the 1816 paper-roll trial and the December 1817 case. Dubois examined a separate manuscript corpus of Necker observations. The British publications and Forbes’s 1822 clinical use document distinct kinds of evidence.

unresolved.about: Recipient of the stethoscope Clark brought from Paris
unresolved.note: Clark’s footnote leaves the recipient unnamed. Read his correspondence with James Johnson and John Forbes to identify the recipient and establish whether the gift overlapped with the journal editor’s acquisition.

evidence.supports: The donor reports a gift to an unnamed English physician.
The unnamed editor’s note reports acquiring cylinders from Paris without identifying a supplier.
